title: The Woman on the Boat
voice: female, ~66, warm Midwestern (Ohio), plainspoken, a little wry, unhurried
background: 8-second clip filmed at eye level from the open top deck of a river cruise ship moving slowly down a calm European river in autumn. Straight ahead across the water, a low riverbank with a small village of white houses and a vineyard hillside behind it. The horizon is level and the river is flat and horizontal. caption: I paid $4,800 for a Rhine cruise and got off the boat at 3 of 7 ports. A 74-year-old woman with a bad hip got off at every single one. On the last night she told me why.
headline: Why I Stayed On The Boat
script:
Seven ports on the Rhine. I got off the boat for three of them.

I paid four thousand eight hundred dollars to watch Germany slide past a window.

And the worst part wasn't my feet. It was a seventy-four-year-old woman from Wisconsin who got off at every port. On the last night, she told me why. I didn't believe her for a year.

Let me back up.

My name is Darlene. I'm sixty-six. I worked a post office counter for thirty-one years, so I thought I knew tired feet.

When my husband passed, my sister Pat said, we are taking that river cruise he never wanted to take. So I bought the shoes everybody tells you to buy.

Hokas. The big ones. A hundred and sixty-five dollars. For the first two hours in Amsterdam, honestly, wonderful.

Then the cobblestones. My foot rolled side to side on every stone, and all that tall foam did nothing for it. And they're heavy. By dinner, my knees hurt worse than my feet.

At the third port I switched to my backup pair. Skechers Memory Foam, about seventy dollars. Soft in the morning, no argument.

By lunch the foam had squashed flat. It doesn't come back until you take them off at night.

So right when the group started up the hill to the castle, I had the least support of the day.

I made it halfway. I sat on a bench by the river and watched the tour flags go up that hill without me.

After that, I mostly stayed on the boat.

That's how I met Margaret. Seventy-four, a bad hip, and she came back from every port pink in the cheeks.

On the last night, I asked her how.

She looked at my Hokas under the deck chair and said, honey, those were made for running down a flat road. You're walking on rocks for eight hours.

Then she said the thing I didn't believe. My shoes cost less than half of yours.

A day in an old town isn't running, and it isn't standing at a counter. Your foot rolls, climbs and swells, hour after hour.

Cushion that only works straight down can't help you on stones. Foam that packs flat by lunch quits on you. And a snug shoe turns into a vise once your feet swell.

So you need five things. A sole firm enough for stones but still bendy. Arch support built into the shoe. A wide toe box. A top that stretches when your feet swell. And light.

I wrote those five things on the back of my boarding pass. Old post office habit.

At home, only one shoe matched all five. Comfort Wear, the Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe. About sixty dollars.

I almost didn't order them. How does sixty dollars beat a hundred and sixty-five?

The first week, honestly, they felt firmer than my Hokas. Less squish. I thought, well, they're fine.

Then I walked our brick downtown for three hours, curbs and courthouse hill included. My feet felt the same at the end as at the start.

So this October, Pat and I booked the Rhine again. Same seven ports.

I got off at all seven.

On the wet stones after the rain, the grip held. At hour nine, when my feet swelled, the knit just gave. The arch was still there after dinner.

One day we did twenty-one thousand steps. My feet didn't hurt. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

And at that castle, I walked right past my old bench. A woman was sitting on it, rubbing her feet, watching the tour flags go up the hill.

I almost stopped to give her Margaret's speech. Then I remembered I had a castle to climb. So I'm giving it to you instead.

Big expensive running shoes were built for a flat road, not a day on old stones.

Comfort Wear's Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe was built for the walking you actually do on a trip.

caption: My daughter took 412 pictures on our trip to Paris. I'm in 11 of them, and in every one I'm sitting down. Then she found the receipt that explained why.
headline: The Worst Travel Advice I Ever Got
script:
My daughter took four hundred and twelve pictures in Paris. I'm in eleven of them.

In every single one, I'm sitting down.

On a bench. On a curb. On the edge of a fountain with my shoes off. That's just where I was.

There's one picture of me I did frame, though. She took it this June. I'll tell you about it at the end.

Let me back up.

I'm Renee. I'm forty-eight, a single mom, and I run the front office at a dental practice. Which means I sit for a living.

When Kayla was six, I promised her Paris for her senior trip. I saved for eleven years. Twenty dollars here, forty there.

Everybody gave me the same advice. Wear your comfortable sneakers. Worst travel advice I ever got.

I bought Hokas, the big ones, a hundred and sixty-five dollars. I packed my Nike Air Max as backup.

Day one, the Hokas felt great for about two hours. Then we hit the cobblestones.

My foot rolled side to side on every stone, and all that thick foam did nothing for it.

And they're heavy. By evening my knees hurt more than my feet.

Day two, I tried the Nikes. Comfortable at home. But after a nine-hour flight and a day of walking, my feet had swelled.

That narrow toe box squeezed like a fist. By hour five, I wasn't tired. I felt beaten up.

So I sat. I sat outside the museum while she went in. I sat at the bottom of the hill while she climbed it. Kayla kept saying, it's fine, Mom.

It wasn't fine. I'd waited eleven years to watch her see Paris, and I was watching from benches.

On the flight home, she went through my receipts for her budgeting app and found the Hoka one.

She looked at me and said, Mom. You bought running shoes for a walking trip.

I said, what's the difference?

She had already looked it up. Running shoes are built for flat roads, for an hour. Cushion that pushes straight down. A shape that's fine until your feet swell.

But a day in an old city is eight, nine, ten hours. Your foot rolls on stones, climbs stairs, stands in lines. And it swells all afternoon.

So she made me a list on an airline napkin.

A sole firm enough for cobblestones, but flexible. Arch support built into the shoe. A wide toe box. A top that stretches when your feet swell. And light.

I put it on my fridge and forgot about it. For a year.

Then she got into a study abroad program in Dublin, and I booked a flight.

Two months before, I found that napkin. I searched every item on it. One shoe checked all five.

Comfort Wear, the Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe. Around sixty dollars.

I laughed. I'd spent a hundred and sixty-five on the pair that put me on a bench.

The first week, I'll be honest, they felt firmer than the Hokas. Less squish.

Then I wore them to the outlet mall. Six hours. I drove home and realized I hadn't once looked for a place to sit.

In Dublin, it rained four days out of six. The grip held on every wet stone.

By evening my feet swelled like always, but the knit just gave. And the arch was still there walking back from dinner.

One day we did twenty-three thousand steps. My feet didn't hurt. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

On our last day, we walked a cliff path outside the city. At the top, Kayla said, Mom, stop. Turn around.

That's the picture I framed. Me standing. Windblown, out of breath, grinning like an idiot. She texted it to me with two words. Who's this?

Running shoes were built for a flat road, not a day on cobblestones.

title: Standing Isn't Walking
voice: female, ~59, warm Texas drawl, brassy and funny, quick laugh, confident
background: 8-second handheld vertical iPhone clip inside a small, busy hair salon on a weekday afternoon: a stylist seen from behind in black scrubs and comfortable shoes working on a client's foils at a station mirror (faces not visible or turned away), a second stylist blow-drying in the background, rolling cart of brushes, warm overhead light, hair-dryer hum and soft chatter. caption: I've stood behind a salon chair 10 hours a day for 34 years. Then I tried to walk 4 miles to train for Rome and called my husband to come get me. A client with foils in her hair told me what I'd gotten wrong.
headline: Standing Shoes Won't Get You Through Rome
script:
I've stood behind a salon chair ten hours a day for thirty-four years. My feet have never once quit on me.

Then, nine weeks before Rome, I tried to walk four miles. At mile three, I called my husband to come get me in the truck.

He pulled up, rolled down the window and said, Glory, how are you going to do Rome?

I didn't have an answer. The answer came from a woman in my chair with foils in her hair.

Let me back up.

I'm Gloria. I'm fifty-nine, and I own a little salon outside San Antonio. Three of my girls and I had been saving for two years to do Rome for my sixtieth.

I figured I was the last person who needed to worry about her feet. I'm on them all day.

So I started training. First walk, I wore my salon clogs. A hundred and fifty dollars, and I'd stand in them all day without thinking.

Walking in them was a different story. Every step, my heel slid and my toes gripped. A mile in, my shins burned.

So I bought Skechers Memory Foam, about seventy dollars. Soft in the morning, no argument.

But by mile two, the foam had pressed flat under me, and it doesn't come back until you take them off at night.

Then I went big. Hokas. A hundred and sixty-five dollars. The first two miles felt great.

But on the old brick path downtown my foot rolled side to side, and all that thick foam gave me nothing for it. And they're heavy. That's the walk that ended in the truck.

The next morning I had Joanne in my chair. Seventy-one, and she led walking tours in Italy for almost twenty years.

I told her the truck story. She laughed so hard I nearly dripped color on her ear.

Then she said, honey, standing and walking are two different jobs.

When you stand, she said, your feet hold still. Clogs and soft foam are fine for that. When you walk, your foot rolls, pushes and bends thousands of times.

And Rome is the worst kind of walking. Cobblestones, old stairs, standing in lines, eight, nine, ten hours.

Running shoes cushion straight down, like on a flat road. Memory foam gives up by early afternoon. And by evening your feet swell and the shoe pinches.

She told me what she wore for twenty years of tours. I wrote it on the back of an appointment card.

A sole firm enough for cobblestones, but flexible. Arch support built into the shoe. A wide toe box. A top that stretches as your feet swell. And light.

Then she said, mine are Comfort Wear. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe. And they cost less than your color appointment.

About sixty dollars. I'd just spent a hundred and sixty-five on the pair that put me in the truck.

The first week, I'll be honest, they felt firmer than the Hokas. Less squish. I wore them in the salon and thought, well, they're fine.

Then I took them on my four-mile route. I finished it. Then I walked it again the next Sunday, plus two.

We landed in Rome in April.

Day two, we did twenty-two thousand steps. Cobblestones, those big stairs, a long line at the museum. My feet didn't hurt. Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

On the wet stones after a rainstorm, the grip held. Every evening my feet swelled, and the knit just gave.

On the last night, we climbed a hill to watch the city light up. My girls sat down. I stayed standing.

I sent Ray a photo of the view. He wrote back, want me to come get you?

I wrote back, not a chance.

My salon clogs were made for standing still. Running shoes were made for a flat road. Neither one was made for Rome.

alt_hooks: Nine weeks before my sixtieth-birthday trip to Rome, my husband had to pick me up off a bench in the truck. I'd made it three miles. I've stood ten hours a day for thirty-four years, and I couldn't walk four.
